judgement.reason: It shows a teacher passing on prophetic and apostolic teaching but does not directly name the sources linking the community to Jesus.
It states the Word was made man so we might be made God, which says who Jesus was for the tradition.
It speaks of the Word made man for human sharing in God but does not set out Jesus's status relative to the Father and Spirit.
It is evidence for one bishop settling one dispute by open argument, not for the whole teacher-bishop-council process.
It bears on God's purpose in pain but addresses suffering, not God's character and nature as a whole.
It shows a teacher who questioned a student, but it is not about someone struggling to believe.
It praises a teacher who drew on prophetic and apostolic teaching but does not state the approach or purpose of reading.
It says Scripture has body, soul and spirit, pointing to depth the reader may miss.
It says only what agrees with apostolic tradition in the churches is truth, so it answers whether other authority stood beside Scripture.
It shows the failure itself, Demetrius against Origen, as told by Eusebius, not how the community responded to it.
It speaks of teaching handed down from the apostles, not of the rituals the visitor asked about.
It speaks of the Word curing disordered passions by urging, which bears on a restless soul but is one teacher's picture, not an answer about unsettled minds.
It shows a few practical rulings from the 380s, not a typical day.
It speaks of holding wealth lightly, one teacher's sermon, not of what people gave up to belong.
Only one question touches marriage, and that one is about an incestuous marriage in the 380s.
It tells the wound from Eusebius's side, not the community's own sense of being unsettled.
It speaks of philosophy as preparation for the Greeks, a nearby question, not the eternal fate of outsiders.
